subject: Physics
title: Introduction to Physics — Scope and Branches
content:
Physics is the study of matter, energy and how they interact. It explains why things move, fall, heat up, light up and conduct electricity.

Main branches you will meet in SS1–SS3: Mechanics (motion & forces), Heat/Thermal physics, Waves (light & sound), Electricity & Magnetism, and Modern physics.

Why it matters: everything from a phone charger to a generating set works on physics principles. Physics also trains you to measure carefully and think logically — the exact skill that wins exam marks.
keyPoints: Physics = matter + energy + their interactions
5 main branches: mechanics, heat, waves, electricity, modern physics
Measurement and units are the foundation of everything in physics

subject: Physics
title: Measurement and Units
content:
Every measurement has a number AND a unit. The SI system (Système International) gives us standard base units:

• Length — metre (m)
• Mass — kilogram (kg)
• Time — second (s)
• Electric current — ampere (A)
• Temperature — kelvin (K)

Derived units are combinations: speed = m/s, force = kg·m/s² = newton (N), work/energy = joule (J).

Scientific notation for very large/small numbers: 0.00045 m = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ m. Prefixes: k = ×1000, m = ×0.001, M = ×1,000,000.

Measuring instruments: metre rule (length), vernier callipers (0.01 cm precision), micrometer screw gauge (0.01 mm precision), stopclock (time).
keyPoints: Always write number + unit
SI base units: m, kg, s, A, K
Vernier callipers: 0.01 cm; micrometer: 0.01 mm

subject: Physics
title: Scalars and Vectors
content:
A scalar has only size (magnitude): mass, distance, speed, time, temperature, energy.
A vector has size AND direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight.

Example: walking 5 m east then 5 m west — distance travelled = 10 m (scalar), but displacement = 0 (vector, direction matters).

Vectors add tip-to-tail. Two vectors at right angles combine by Pythagoras: R = √(x² + y²).
keyPoints: Scalar = size only; Vector = size + direction
Distance is scalar, displacement is vector
Resultant of perpendicular vectors: R = √(x² + y²)

subject: Physics
title: Motion — Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
content:
Speed = distance ÷ time (scalar). Velocity = displacement ÷ time (vector).
Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken, unit m/s².

Equations of uniformly accelerated motion (must memorise!):
1) v = u + at
2) s = ut + ½at²
3) v² = u² + 2as

where u = initial velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, s = distance, t = time.

Worked example: A car starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² for 5 s. Final velocity v = u + at = 0 + (2)(5) = 10 m/s. Distance s = ut + ½at² = 0 + ½(2)(25) = 25 m.

Distance–time graphs: gradient = speed. Velocity–time graphs: gradient = acceleration; area under graph = distance.
keyPoints: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as
Gradient of v–t graph = acceleration; area under = distance
Free fall: a = g = 10 m/s² (approx.)

subject: Physics
title: Newton's Laws of Motion
content:
First law (inertia): a body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force. That's why you jerk forward when a bus brakes!

Second law: Force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). 1 newton gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s².

Third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite — the rocket pushes gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up.

Weight W = mg (mass × gravitational acceleration, g ≈ 10 m/s² on Earth). Weight is a force (vector), mass is scalar.

Worked example: F = ma — a 4 kg object accelerates at 3 m/s², so F = 4 × 3 = 12 N.
keyPoints: 1st: inertia — no resultant force, no change in motion
2nd: F = ma
3rd: equal and opposite reaction; W = mg

subject: Physics
title: Work, Energy and Power
content:
Work = Force × distance moved in the direction of the force. Unit: joule (J). If you push a wall and it doesn't move, work = 0!

Energy = ability to do work. Kinetic energy (motion): KE = ½mv². Potential energy (position): PE = mgh.

Principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed. A falling object converts PE → KE.

Power = work done ÷ time taken. Unit: watt (W) = J/s.

Worked example: a 2 kg ball lifted 5 m gains PE = mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J.
keyPoints: W = F × d (joules)
KE = ½mv²; PE = mgh
Power = W/t (watts)

subject: Physics
title: Heat Energy — Temperature and Heat Transfer
content:
Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature tells how hot a body is. Unit of temperature: °C or K (0°C = 273 K).

Three ways heat travels:
1. Conduction — through solids, particles vibrate and pass energy along (metals are best conductors)
2. Convection — in liquids and gases, hot fluid rises, cool fluid sinks (sea breeze!)
3. Radiation — infrared waves, needs no medium (heat from the sun)

Thermometers: liquid-in-glass (mercury/alcohol), clinical, thermocouple.
keyPoints: Heat = energy in transit; temperature = degree of hotness
Conduction, convection, radiation

subject: Physics
title: Light — Reflection
content:
Light travels in straight lines (rectilinear propagation). When it hits a mirror it reflects.

Laws of reflection:
1. Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (i = r)
2. Incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane.

Plane mirror image properties: same size as object, upright (erect), virtual, laterally inverted (left becomes right), as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

Uses: periscope, kaleidoscope, car mirrors (convex for wide view).
keyPoints: i = r (angles measured from the normal)
Plane mirror images: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
Regular vs diffuse (irregular) reflection

subject: Physics
title: Light — Refraction
content:
Refraction = bending of light as it passes between media of different optical density (air → water → glass).

Laws of refraction:
1. Incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane.
2. Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r (constant for the two media).

Refractive index n = c/v — speed of light in vacuum divided by speed in the medium. Glass ≈ 1.5, water ≈ 1.33.

Effects: a swimming pool looks shallower than it is; a spoon in water looks bent; light entering glass bends TOWARD the normal, leaving it bends AWAY.
keyPoints: Light bends at a boundary between different media
Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r
n = c/v; bigger n = denser optically
